p.title: The partisan ties of lobbying firms

ext.title: The partisan ties of lobbying firms
ext.venue: Research & Politics, July-September 2019, pp. 1-9 (volume and issue not stated in the extracted text)
ext.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; empirical quantitative study (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 1,151 lines of the extracted text file (front matter, abstract, introduction, theory, research design, descriptive statistics, Tables 1-3, difference-in-differences results, conclusion, acknowledgements, funding, references). Figures 1-4 are covered through captions and surrounding text only. Online Appendices A-G and replication files are cited but not in the extracted text, so their contents are not covered. Paul's markup: the single annotation file was read; it holds 24 highlights, all with empty note text. Metadata hint corrected: the hint left authors blank (three authors now listed); title, year, venue and DOI in the hint were confirmed.
ext.research_question: Do partisan ties between US lobbying firms and the partisan leadership of Congress raise the revenue those firms earn from clients? Are lobbying firms institutions with relatively stable partisan identities, and do ties to House and Senate majorities return different amounts (abstract; pp.1-2)?
ext.theory: A partisan theory of legislative subsidy. Legislators have scarce time and staff and gain from lobbyists' information, intelligence and labor (Hall and Deardorff 2006). Legislators trust their closest allies, and in a polarized era allies are mostly co-partisans, so a firm's partisan organizational identity signals that it is an ally (p.2). Majority status gives access that outside interests pay more for (Cox and Magar 1999), so co-partisanship with the chamber majority should raise client payments (p.2). H1: firms with partisan ties to the majority party earn more than firms without such ties. H2: partisan ties to the House majority return more than ties to the Senate majority, plausibly because Senate staffing is larger per member, so clients pay less for Senate lobbying (pp.2-3). Baker (2008) interviews add a second account: lobbyists view senators as harder to lobby (cross-pressured, broad-interest, less attentive to detail) (p.3). Firm-level controls (client count, client diversity, law-firm status, international offices, domestic offices, age) are expected to shape prestige, risk spreading and scale economies (p.3).
ext.identification: Two strategies. (1) Panel regressions with firm random effects and year fixed effects; the authors note Senate effects may be suppressed by multicollinearity (Online Appendix C, not in extracted text). (2) First differences (Change in revenue on change in X), which removes residual unobserved firm heterogeneity and time-invariant covariates (p.6). For causation, the authors treat changes in chamber control as exogenous interventions: the 2011 House takeover by Republicans (Tea Party period) and the 2015 Senate takeover by Republicans. They use kernel-weighted difference-in-differences (Hazlett 2019) comparing firms aligned with the party gaining control against firms aligned with the ousted party (p.7). Argument: firms would not be newly founded as in-party firms right after a takeover, so year-over-year changes are attributed to perceived in-party value; switching of lobbyists between opposite-party firms is said to be ruled out in Online Appendix F (not in extracted text). The text reports no explicit parallel-trends check in the main text.
ext.data: Unbalanced quarterly panel of 1,603 lobbying firms, Q1 2008 to Q3 2016 (unit: firm-quarter; N = 33,243; T = 2 to 35 quarters per firm; Table 2). Sources: public Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) reports (reporting became quarterly after HLOGA 2007); campaign contributions by each firm's lobbyists back to 1990; firm websites for law-firm status (2015), international office (2015), number of domestic offices and firm age. Website covariates are missing for firms without sites (smaller, newer and disbanded firms most at risk) and were multiply imputed (King et al. 2001; Online Appendix A). Sample rule: registrant differs from client (contract lobbyist); at least two active lobbyists in the same quarter at least once; at least two quarters with nonzero dollars. About 84% of firms had nonzero campaign giving (p.4). Dependent variable: revenue per lobbyist per quarter, in real dollars (CPI-U). Table 1: mean US$74,007 (SD 71,481), median US$54,365, range US$776 to US$913,800. Replication data: Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/3HDSM8.
ext.method: Two sets of linear panel models. Set 1 (levels, Table 2, models 1.1-1.6): revenue per lobbyist regressed on House alignment and Senate alignment, crossed as time-fixed vs time-varying partisanship and 85%, 90% and 95% giving thresholds, plus controls (number of clients, client diversity = Simpson reciprocal diversity of issues plus industries, law firm, international office, domestic offices, firm age). Firm random effects, year fixed effects, HC3 Arellano standard errors clustered by firm. H2 tested with a restricted F-test that the House and Senate coefficients are equal. Set 2 (first differences, Table 3, models 2.1-2.6): change in revenue on change in alignment, clients and diversity. Partisan measure: a firm is aligned with a chamber's leadership party if its lobbyists' contributions exceed the threshold share to that party; bipartisan or unclear firms are coded as aligned with neither chamber (p.3). Reliability: Fleiss kappa 0.86 (time-fixed) and 0.84 (time-varying). Validity: correlations of 0.31 to 0.55 between contribution-based partisanship and founder-based partisanship (web pages); time-fixed vs time-varying correlation 0.62 to 0.63 (p.3). Causal test: kernel-weighted difference-in-differences (Hazlett 2019) around the 2011 and 2015 takeovers (p.7-8).
ext.scope: US federal contract lobbying firms (registrants that act as contract lobbyists for clients) that meet the LDA sample rules, reporting 2008-2016, after the 2007 HLOGA quarterly-reporting change. Institutions: the House and Senate party leadership. Not a census of all lobbying firms or of in-house lobbying; the 1,603 firms are the sample that met the rules. Individual lobbyists are not the unit of analysis; the firm is (p.1-2, p.8).
measures: Revenue per Lobbyist per Quarter (dependent; real US$, CPI-U adjusted; sum of client income divided by lobbyists)
Firm Partisan Alignment with House Leadership (binary; 1 if the firm's partisan identity matches House leadership)
Firm Partisan Alignment with Senate Leadership (binary; same logic for Senate leadership)
Partisan threshold: 85%, 90% or 95% of lobbyists' contributions to one party
Time-fixed partisan identity (based on contributions dating to 1990) vs time-varying identity (updated yearly from roster and giving)
Number of Clients (unique entities lobbied for; mean 10.36, median 4, max 276)
Client Diversity (Simpson reciprocal index for issues and industries, summed; mean 9.25)
Law Firm, International Office (2015 status, websites); Number of Domestic Offices; Firm Age (observed year minus founding year; mean 18.31)
Founder-based partisanship (for validity check; Democratic, Republican or bipartisan founders)
Change-in-variables versions of all of the above for first-difference models
Takeover treatment indicator for difference-in-differences (aligned with gaining party vs ousted party)

key_findings.finding: Partisan identities of lobbying firms are relatively stable and reliable (kappa and time-fixed/time-varying correlation); founder-based partisanship correlates with contribution-based partisanship.
key_findings.numbers: Fleiss kappa 0.86 time-fixed, 0.84 time-varying; correlations 0.62-0.63 across measures; founder correlations 0.31-0.55 (p<=0.05)

key_findings.finding: Roughly 42-60% of firms are partisan and 40-58% bipartisan, depending on the cutoff; the share distribution is bimodal, with a drop-off after the 95% threshold.
key_findings.numbers: 42-60% partisan; 40-58% bipartisan; 84% of firms had nonzero giving

key_findings.finding: Bipartisan firms consistently earned more average revenue than partisan-leaning firms; Democratic and Republican firms were at rough parity, with a small advantage that shifted with congressional control; unclassified firms earned least.
key_findings.numbers: No point estimates in text; Democratic firms led 2008-2010, Republican firms 2011-2016

key_findings.finding: House partisan alignment is significantly and positively associated with firm revenue in all six panel models (H1 supported for the House).
key_findings.numbers: Time-fixed coefficients 5,536 (SE 1,734), 6,527 (1,944), 6,096 (2,132); time-varying 5,148 (1,298), 5,346 (1,343), 4,940 (1,396); all p<=0.05. Text: about US$5,000-6,000 per lobbyist per quarter

key_findings.finding: Senate partisan alignment is significant only with the time-fixed measure, and not with the time-varying measure, so H1 for the Senate is specification-dependent.
The restricted test of equal House and Senate effects (H2) is significant only with time-varying measures.
Changes in House alignment are associated with changes in revenue (first differences); H1 holds for the House in five of six models, with one model just short of conventional significance.
key_findings.numbers: Time-fixed change coefficients 3,520*, 3,638*, 5,048*; time-varying 1,819*, 1,741 (p~0.07), 2,370*; text range US$1,800-5,000 per lobbyist per quarter. No Senate support in first differences

key_findings.finding: Partisan ties to the House are more revenue-enhancing than Senate ties in only two of six first-difference models.
key_findings.numbers: Restricted F significant in models 2.4 (4*) and 2.6 (4*); others 1-3, not significant

key_findings.finding: Controls: number of clients is positive and significant; client diversity is positive and significant in levels but not in first differences; law firm status is strongly negative; international office, domestic offices and firm age are mostly not significant.
key_findings.numbers: Number of Clients about 1,650 per lobbyist per quarter (significant); Client Diversity about 1,310 (significant); Law Firm -5,529* to -6,172* (significant); Change in Client Diversity not significant

key_findings.finding: When Republicans regained the House in 2011, Republican-aligned firms gained and Democratic-aligned firms lost revenue (difference-in-differences; the strongest causal evidence in the paper).
key_findings.location: p.7-8 (Figure 3; text on Tea Party-era takeover)
key_findings.numbers: Republican-aligned firms gained just over US$10,000 for the year; ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than US$40,000 in annual revenue, despite the Democrats keeping the Senate

key_findings.finding: The 2015 Republican takeover of the Senate produced no significant revenue effects in the difference-in-differences design.
key_findings.location: p.8 (Figure 4; Online Appendix G for details)
key_findings.numbers: No significant effects reported in text; figure values not in extracted text

key_findings.finding: Tally across tests: House ties support the revenue hypothesis in 12 of 13 tests; Senate ties in only 3 of 13; House-over-Senate advantage in 5 of 12 tests.

Authors' interpretation: partisan ties with the House are a more reliable revenue source than Senate ties, possibly reflecting staffing differences; alternative explanations (longer electoral cycle, supermajority rules, member prominence in the Senate) are not tested. Moosbrugger (2012) suggested as a starting point.

limitations: Senate evidence is mixed and depends on model specification (time-fixed vs time-varying; threshold); the authors say support for H1 for the Senate would be somewhat higher if multicollinearity in models 1.4-1.6 were considered (p.8; Online Appendix C).
The House-over-Senate difference is attributed to staffing differences, but the authors name untested alternatives (electoral cycle, supermajority rules, member prominence) (p.8).
Firm characteristics from websites are missing for firms without sites; smaller, newer and disbanded firms are most at risk; missing values are multiply imputed (p.3, p.5).
The partisan boundary (partisan vs bipartisan) is acknowledged as fuzzy; the authors therefore use three cutoffs and two measures (p.3).
Founder-based validation is a correlation check on the contribution-based measure, not an independent causal test (p.3).
Model 2.5 (time-varying, 85% threshold, first differences) falls just short of conventional significance (p.6).

Difference-in-differences rests on two takeover episodes (2011 House, 2015 Senate); the 2015 Senate test shows no effect. The main text does not report a parallel-trends diagnostic; the authors point to Online Appendix G and to Hazlett (2019) for the estimator.
The 2019 lobbying data were not yet available; the authors plan to re-test after the 2018 midterm switch of House control (p.8).
Causal claims rely on the argument that firms are not newly formed as in-party firms right after a takeover (p.7); the paper states this as a plausibility argument.

short_quotes.quote: lobbying firms themselves are institutions with relatively stable partisan identities

rel.summary_md:
Furnas, Heaney and LaPira (2019) ask whether US contract lobbying firms have stable partisan identities and whether ties to the majority party raise their revenue. The sample is 1,603 LDA contract registrants observed by quarter from 2008 Q1 to 2016 Q3 (33,243 firm-quarters). A firm's partisanship comes from the share of its lobbyists' FEC contributions that go to one party, using cutoffs of 85, 90 or 95%. These identities are reliable (Fleiss kappa 0.84 to 0.86). Between 42% and 60% of firms are partisan, and bipartisan firms earn the highest average revenue.

The outcome is real revenue per lobbyist per quarter, with a mean of $74k. In all six levels models, alignment with the House majority adds about $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter. Senate alignment matters only under the time-fixed measure. A kernel-weighted difference-in-differences around the 2011 House flip finds that Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10k over the year while Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect. Across all tests, House ties support the revenue hypothesis in 12 of 13 and Senate ties in 3 of 13.

For Paul's systems, the main relevance is to the Mentat sector-growth and lobbying-forecast lanes, not to the Melange engine. The study supports keeping House and Senate separate and expecting a weaker Senate signal. It measures a premium clients are willing to pay for perceived access to the majority. That is a market valuation: it is not a measure of persuasion and not an access probability. The effect is also distributional: control changes move revenue between partisan firms. The paper does not estimate how sector totals respond, which is the level Mentat's lobbying model works at. This reading is UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: House-majority ties raise contract-firm revenue in 12 of 13 tests; Senate ties in only 3 of 13. In the 2011 House-flip difference-in-differences, Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10k and ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k in annual revenue. Both figures are firm-level, one-year windows, on a revenue-per-lobbyist outcome. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect.
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W keeps House and Senate on separate seat scales (sgs_seats.R:24). The brain records one election, the 2022 House, over 17 weeks: -3.47 pp in the Democratic share of giving per +1 expected Democratic seat (block bootstrap p .0086 to .0174), with the Senate null. The result is EXPLORATORY.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The House-yes, Senate-null pattern in SEATS-W matches the paper's House-over-Senate pattern, which supports keeping chamber-specific estimates. The paper does not predict SEATS-W's sign. It measures contract-lobbying revenue after control has actually changed, by firm partisanship. SEATS-W measures the partisan share of PAC and individual giving as within-cycle seat forecasts move. A party-share drop as expected Democratic seats rise is not explained by majority-access pricing, so the paper cannot be cited as evidence for access-seeking in SEATS-W. Both are single-episode designs: one House flip in the paper, one election in SEATS-W.

bearings.paper_claim: A change in House control moves contract-lobbying revenue between partisan firms. In 2011, Republican-aligned firms gained about $10k and Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k per lobbyist over the year (firm-level difference-in-differences). Democratic firms led in revenue in 2008-2010 and Republican firms in 2011-2016. Bipartisan firms earned the most throughout.
bearings.system_side: The lobbying card reports outside-firm fees (LDA income_total) and in-house expenses separately and never adds them. The lobbying refit is sector-aggregate and has no partisan term: dy ~ dg + factor(year), with the anchor at the last year.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's population, federal contract registrants, is the outside-firm fees series, so the evidence applies to that series and not to in-house expenses. The effect is distributional across firm partisanship. The paper does not identify a sector-total change. A common control shock would be absorbed by factor(year) in the fit, but the forecast cannot include it for future years. Before adding a control-flip term, test whether outside-firm totals step after the 2011, 2015 and 2019 flips. The 2008-2016 era and the HLOGA quarterly regime both apply to the LDA series.

bearings.paper_claim: Majority status carries a revenue premium in the contract-lobbying market of about $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter for House alignment (levels models). The Senate premium depends on specification.
bearings.system_side: The SHIFT tables regress the Republican share of giving on the expected-minus-current control shift. The brain records no stable partisan shift, chamber-stacked: -0.04, p .76. The House estimate is SATURATED and the Senate estimate is -0.16.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The outcomes differ. The paper measures who earns lobbying fees, not where PAC money goes, and Furnas et al. separately show low overlap between organizations that lobby and organizations that give. A null SHIFT on PAC giving share is therefore not contradicted by a revenue premium for lobbying firms. If SHIFT is ever extended to lobbying, the paper suggests keying it to realized House control, with chambers stratified.

gaps_exposed: No firm-level partisan identity for lobbying registrants. Neither Melange nor Mentat derives a registrant's partisanship from its lobbyists' FEC giving, which the paper shows is reliable (kappa 0.84 to 0.86). If added, it may only be a descriptive identity attribute (D-021), never an edge or a weight.
The Mentat lobbying refit (dy ~ dg + factor(year)) has no partisan or control-change term, and the outside-firm fee series has not been checked for steps after House flips (2011, 2019).

No House-versus-Senate stratification for lobbying. The forecast and the sector study split chambers for giving share but not for lobbying revenue, the outcome where the paper finds the House-Senate asymmetry.

The system does not track bipartisan intermediaries among lobbying firms. The paper finds bipartisan firms earn the most, consistent with Bacik's bipartisan-lobbyist finding, but no firm-level bipartisanship measure exists.
flags: Denominator and window: the DV is real revenue per lobbyist per quarter. The 2011 difference-in-differences figures (+$10k Republican-aligned, more than -$40k Democratic-aligned) are one-year changes estimated on that outcome for 1,603 contract firms, 2008-2016. Quote them with that window and denominator, and never as sector totals or as a per-firm figure.

The revenue premium measures what clients pay for perceived majority access. Under D-025 it must not be restated as an access probability, a closeness measure or an influence weight. Under D-021, LDA-derived firm partisanship is identity only.

Citation hygiene: the cpf_pressure comment at fec/moneyball_core.py:10-11 cites 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment'. That is not this paper. This paper offers no persuasion ratio and cannot calibrate the 1.7/0.5 constants.
The paper argues for neither of the rejected SNA proposals (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization).

Paul's seats-weekly position says 'neither paper on disk'. That is stale for this paper, which has now been read in full. His highlight records only the -$40k loss, not the asymmetric +$10k gain, and does not state that the figure is per lobbyist.

The SEATS-W sign is negative: the Democratic giving share falls as expected Democratic seats rise. This paper does not explain that result, so it must not be cited as corroborating access-seeking in SEATS-W.
rel.paul_alignment: The evidence partly agrees with Paul's takeaway. His highlights (stable firm partisanship, a large loss for firms tied to the party that loses the House, weaker Senate ties, very few lobbyists moving between opposite-party firms) match the paper. Two points need correcting. First, the $40k figure is a one-year change on a per-lobbyist outcome and applies to Democratic-aligned firms. The matching gain for Republican-aligned firms was only about $10k, so the effect is asymmetric. Second, the paper concerns lobbying-fee revenue, not PAC giving. Paul's plan uses it, together with Cox & Magar, to motivate the seats test, but SEATS-W found a House response with the opposite sign to a 'chase the expected winner' reading, and SHIFT found no stable partisan shift. The paper therefore supports splitting by chamber, House versus Senate, and does not support the direction of the seat-gain hypothesis. His note that the paper is not on disk is stale, and his annotation entry for this work is empty.

related.why: Bacik finds bipartisan lobbyists and teams earn more while legislators polarize. This paper finds the same bipartisan revenue premium at the level of lobbying firms.
Same first author. It shows low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which explains why a lobbying-revenue premium need not appear in PAC giving-share tests (SHIFT, SEATS).
Both build on LDA disclosure records. This paper uses the registrant-versus-client split to isolate contract firms, the population behind Mentat's outside-firm fees series.
Both infer organizational partisanship or ideology from the contribution records of affiliated individuals.
Kim links campaign donations and lobbying sequentially. This paper uses lobbyists' donations as a partisan identity signal, not as a lobbying predictor.
The review covers Bertrand et al. (2014) on who-you-know versus what-you-know, which this paper extends from individual lobbyists to lobbying firms.
